blocks.q: city = np.array([1, 2, 0, 1]). What does np.mean(city == 1) give?

opts.t: 1, because the first house is red
0.5, the fraction of houses that are red
An error: you can't average booleans

blocks.why: city == 1 is [True, False, False, True]. numpy treats True as 1 and False as 0, so the mean is 2/4 = 0.5. "Mean of a mask" = "fraction that satisfy the condition", a pattern you'll use in every chapter.

    occupied = city[city != 0]
    frac_red = np.mean(occupied == 1)

blocks.html:
Here are the rules, exactly as in the 3D city but on one street:

  1. Each house is empty (0), red (1) or blue (2). The street wraps around.
  2. A household looks at the 2r houses around it. It is happy if at least a fraction p of its occupied neighbours share its colour (or if it has no neighbours at all).
  3. Each step, every unhappy household moves to a random empty house.

blocks.html: Now the step function. Before you write it, rebuild it from scrambled lines. Watch for the decoy.
The full model, with a plot. Run it, then change p to 0.3 and to 0.7.

blocks.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def same_neighbors(city, r=1):
    count = np.zeros(len(city), dtype=int)
    for d in range(-r, r + 1):
        if d != 0:
            count += (np.roll(city, d) == city) & (city != 0)
    return count

def occupied_neighbors(city, r=1):
    count = np.zeros(len(city), dtype=int)
    for d in range(-r, r + 1):
        if d != 0:
            count += np.roll(city, d) != 0
    return count

def unhappy(city, p=0.5, r=1):
    same, occ = same_neighbors(city, r), occupied_neighbors(city, r)
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
        frac = np.where(occ > 0, same / occ, 1.0)
    return (city != 0) & (frac < p)

def step(city, rng, p=0.5, r=1):
    movers = np.flatnonzero(unhappy(city, p, r))
    rng.shuffle(movers)
    for i in movers:
        j = rng.choice(np.flatnonzero(city == 0))
        city[j], city[i] = city[i], 0

def segregation(city, r=2):
    occ = occupied_neighbors(city, r)
    mask = (city != 0) & (occ > 0)
    return np.mean(same_neighbors(city, r)[mask] / occ[mask])

blocks.html: City planners really do ask "if we build this street of new homes, will it stay mixed?" Nobody can run the experiment on real families, but you can run it on your model in a second, a hundred times, with different settings. That is what a what-if tool is: the same model you just wrote, wrapped in a function that answers a planner's question with a number.

blocks.title: Neighbourhood-mix simulator for a city planner
blocks.client: A city housing office planning a new 200-home street
blocks.brief: The planners want a table: for each tolerance level p (how many alike neighbours a household wants), how segregated does the street end up, on average? Your job is to turn the street model into two functions: one that runs a street until it settles, and one that sweeps p and reports the average segregation.
blocks.why: Policy teams, urban-planning consultancies and game studios all build tools like this: a model plus a sweep over the knobs people care about. The same pattern (run until stable, repeat with many random seeds, average) is how A/B-test simulators, epidemic dashboards and load-testing tools work.

blocks.html: Complexity science starts from a set of shifts away from classical, equation-based science. Your street model shows several of them at once: it's discrete (houses, not a smooth density), stochastic (random moves), made of many interacting agents, and studied by computation (you ran it) rather than by analysis (solving for an answer on paper).

blocks.q: Which pair best describes the move from classical models to the Schelling model?

opts.t: From one or two bodies described by equations, to many simple agents studied by simulation

blocks.why: Classical physics models a few bodies with equations you can solve. Schelling's model has hundreds of agents with a simple rule, and the interesting result, strong clustering from mild preferences, appears only when you run it. That is the core shift complexity science describes.

blocks.q: Nobody in the model wants a segregated street (at p = 0.5 everyone is fine with half their neighbours being different). Yet the street segregates. What is the name for a pattern at the level of the whole system that no individual rule mentions?
blocks.why: Emergence: the system-level property (large single-colour blocks) is not written into any agent's rule. You saw it appear in the plot.

blocks.q: In your own words: why does a city segregate strongly even when each household is happy with half its neighbours being different?
blocks.a:
• A household that moves leaves a gap and lands somewhere new, which changes the neighbourhood of several other households.
  • Moves are local and keep cascading: each move can make a neighbour unhappy, who then moves too.
  • The system only stops when (almost) nobody is unhappy, and the configurations where nobody is unhappy are mostly clustered ones. Mild individual preferences + feedback = strong collective pattern.

blocks.q: Why use np.roll instead of a loop with city[i-1] and city[i+1]?
blocks.a:
• It handles the whole array at once (fast, short code).
  • It wraps around, so the ends of the street need no special case: the street is a ring.
  • np.roll(city, d) lines every house up with its neighbour at offset d, so one comparison checks every house.

blocks.q: In an undirected graph with n nodes, how many edges does the complete graph (every node linked to every other) have?

blocks.html: A graph is connected if you can get from any node to any other by following edges. The algorithm: start somewhere, mark it seen, then keep visiting neighbours of things you've seen until there's nothing new.

blocks.title: reachable_nodes, the classic version
blocks.prompt: Rebuild the search. A stack holds nodes we have found but not processed; seen holds nodes we've processed.

blocks.code:
def reachable_nodes(G, start):
    seen = set()
    stack = [start]
    while stack:
        node = stack.pop()
        if node not in seen:
            seen.add(node)
            stack.extend(G.neighbors(node))
    return seen

G = nx.Graph([(0, 1), (1, 2), (3, 4), (5, 5)])
print(sorted(reachable_nodes(G, 2)))
print(sorted(reachable_nodes(G, 5)))
print(len(G), len(reachable_nodes(G, 3)))

blocks.q: Explain how reachable_nodes works, and why it can't loop forever even though the graph has cycles.
blocks.a:
• It keeps a stack of nodes still to process and a set of nodes already processed.
  • Each round it pops a node; if it's new it marks it seen and pushes all its neighbours.
  • Cycles lead back to nodes already in seen, which are popped and skipped, so each node is processed at most once and the loop ends when the stack is empty.
  • The graph is connected exactly when the set it returns contains every node.

blocks.q: What happens to the probability that G(n, p) is connected as p increases, and what's special about ln(n)/n?
blocks.a:
• It stays near 0 for small p, then jumps to near 1 over a narrow range of p: a phase transition.
  • The jump is centred near p\* = ln(n)/n, and it gets sharper as n grows.
  • Intuition: at p\*, the expected number of isolated nodes drops below about one; isolated nodes are the last thing stopping the graph from being connected.

blocks.html:
In 1967 Stanley Milgram asked people in Nebraska to forward a letter to a stranger in Boston, only through people they knew by first name. The letters that arrived took about six hand-offs. That's strange: your friends mostly know each other (a clustered network), and clustered networks usually have long paths, because you keep circling inside your own group.

Watts and Strogatz (1998) explained it with a tiny model: start with a perfectly regular, clustered network, then rewire a few edges at random. This chapter builds that model and measures it.

From the 3D world: in the Village you sent a letter around the lake and then placed a single shortcut. One shortcut cut the trip from many hand-offs to a few. That's the small-world effect, and this chapter measures it. Open the Village

blocks.why: Local clustering means most of your links lead back into your own neighbourhood, so a purely local network has long paths. Milgram's short chains are the surprise this chapter explains.

blocks.html: A ring lattice puts n nodes in a circle and joins each one to its k nearest neighbours (k/2 on each side). It's the most clustered, most "local" network you can draw.

blocks.code:
def adjacent_edges(nodes, halfk):
    n = len(nodes)
    for i, u in enumerate(nodes):
        for j in range(i + 1, i + halfk + 1):
            v = nodes[j % n]
            yield u, v

def make_ring_lattice(n, k):
    G = nx.Graph()
    nodes = range(n)
    G.add_nodes_from(nodes)
    G.add_edges_from(adjacent_edges(nodes, k // 2))
    return G

blocks.html:
reachable_nodes from chapter 2 used a stack (last in, first out), so it plunges deep before coming back: depth-first. Swap the stack for a queue (first in, first out) and the search spreads out in rings: first everything one step away, then two steps, and so on. That's breadth-first search (BFS), and it's exactly what you need for shortest paths.

A Python list is slow at removing from the front, so we use collections.deque, which is fast at both ends.

blocks.q: Explain why a few random shortcuts make paths short but leave clustering high.
blocks.a:
• Path length is a global property: one shortcut between distant parts of the ring gives a fast route to everyone near either end, so the average over all pairs drops a lot.
  • Clustering is local: each shortcut destroys only the few triangles that used the edge it replaced. With p = 0.01, about 99% of edges, and almost all triangles, are untouched.
  • So there's a wide range of p where the network is both clustered (like a lattice) and short (like a random graph): a small world.

blocks.q: What's the one change that turns depth-first search into breadth-first search, and why does BFS give shortest paths?
blocks.a:
• Replace the stack (pop from the end) with a queue (pop from the front, deque.popleft).
  • BFS processes nodes in order of distance: all nodes at distance 1, then 2, and so on. So the first time a node is discovered, it's along a shortest path, and its distance is its parent's + 1.

sections.title: Heavy tails on a log-log plot

blocks.html: On ordinary axes a heavy tail is invisible: it's a long, flat line near zero. On log-log axes, a power law PMF(k) ∝ k^(−α) becomes a straight line with slope −α. Compare the WS graph with NetworkX's built-in Barabási–Albert graph (which you're about to write yourself).

blocks.title: Two degree distributions, log-log

All nodes have the same degree

blocks.why: log PMF = −α log k + c is a straight line on log-log axes, which is the same as PMF(k) ∝ k^(−α): a power law. For the BA model α is about 3.

blocks.html:
Barabási and Albert's idea, which you played as the Town's lottery:

  1. Growth: start with k nodes; add new nodes one at a time.
  2. Preferential attachment: each new node links to k existing nodes, chosen with probability proportional to their degree.

The trick for "proportional to degree" is lovely: keep a list, repeated_nodes, where every node appears once per edge it has. Picking uniformly from that list picks nodes in proportion to degree.

sections.title: Real-world project: which hub airports matter most?

blocks.html: Airline routes, the internet's routers and protein networks in your cells all have hubs. Here you'll measure that, using the BA graphs you just built as a stand-in for a route map.

def _random_subset(repeated_nodes, k):

def barabasi_albert_graph(n, k):

blocks.q: Why does the BA model produce hubs while the WS model doesn't? Mention both ingredients.
blocks.a:
• WS starts from a lattice where every node has degree k and rewires a few edges, so degrees stay close to k.
  • BA has growth (old nodes have had more time to collect links) and preferential attachment (high-degree nodes are more likely to get the next link).
  • Together they create a feedback loop: being big makes you grow faster. The result is a power-law degree distribution with a few huge hubs.
  • Remove preferential attachment (uniform choice) and the tail becomes exponential: no hubs.

blocks.q: What does the repeated_nodes list contain, and why does choosing from it uniformly implement preferential attachment?
blocks.a:
• Every node appears in the list once for each edge it has (both ends of every edge get added).
  • So a node with degree d occupies d slots, and a uniform random pick lands on it with probability d / (total degree): proportional to degree.
  • It avoids computing probabilities explicitly; updating the list is just extend.

chapters.title: Cellular automata
chapters.tagline: A row of cells, eight-entry rule tables, and the strange worlds of rules 30 and 110
goals: Turn a rule number like 30 into its rule table with binary
Compute a whole new row at once with np.correlate and a window of [4, 2, 1]
Run any elementary CA and sort its behaviour into Wolfram's four classes
Use Rule 30's centre column as a pseudo-random bit generator
chapters.prelude:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

blocks.html:
A cellular automaton (CA) is a world reduced to the bare minimum:

  • cells in a row (or grid),
  • each in one of a few states (here 0 or 1),
  • a rule that gives a cell's next state from its own state and its neighbours',
  • discrete time: every cell updates at once, step after step.

Wolfram's elementary CAs use a 1-D row and look at three cells: left, self, right. Three cells of 0/1 give 2³ = 8 possible neighbourhoods, so a rule is just a table of 8 output bits. Read those 8 bits as a binary number and you get the rule's name: Rule 0 to Rule 255.

From the 3D world: in Automata you predicted the next row by hand, wrote your own rule table, and sorted rules 0, 18, 30 and 110 into classes. Here you make the computer do the same work. Open Automata

blocks.q: How many different elementary CA rules are there?
blocks.why: Each of the 8 neighbourhoods can map to 0 or 1, so there are 2⁸ = 256 rule tables, named Rule 0 to Rule 255.

sections.title: From a rule number to a rule table

blocks.title: Rules 50, 30 and 110

blocks.html: Change the rules. Try 18, 90, 54, 73, 184.

Wolfram sorted the 256 rules by what they do from a random start:

ClassBehaviourExample
1Everything dies out to a uniform stateRule 0
2Simple, stable or repeating structuresRule 50
3Chaotic, random-looking foreverRule 30
4Localised structures that move and interact: neither order nor chaosRule 110

Rule 110 is Turing complete: with the right starting row it can compute anything a computer can. Simple rules, universal computation.

sections.title: Real-world project: fair dice from Rule 30

blocks.html: You have random-looking bits. A board-game app needs dice rolls: whole numbers 1 to 6, each equally likely. Turning bits into fair numbers is a real job with a classic trap, and checking that the result is fair needs a real statistical test. Both are things working programmers do whenever they touch random numbers.

blocks.title: A dice roller and fairness checker built on Rule 30
blocks.client: A small studio making a digital board game
blocks.brief: Turn Rule 30's centre column into die rolls, and build a fairness check the studio can run in its test suite. Three bits make a number from 0 to 7. The obvious trick, value % 6 + 1, is unfair: 0 and 1 and 6 and 7 all land on faces 1 and 2, so those faces come up twice as often. The fix is rejection sampling: throw away 6 and 7 and use the next three bits.
blocks.why: Every language's standard library does this: Python's random.randrange, Java's nextInt(bound) and Go's rand.Intn reject values instead of using %, because modulo bias is a real bug (it has broken online poker shuffles and password generators). Chi-square tests like the one you'll write are how casinos, lotteries and game studios prove to regulators that their randomness is fair.

blocks.solution:
def run_ca(rule, n_rows, width):
    table = np.unpackbits(np.array([rule], dtype=np.uint8))[::-1]
    array = np.zeros((n_rows, width), dtype=np.uint8)
    array[0, width // 2] = 1
    for i in range(1, n_rows):
        c = np.correlate(array[i - 1], [4, 2, 1], mode="same")
        array[i] = table[c]
    return array

blocks.q: Walk through how one row of an elementary CA is computed with numpy, from rule number to new row.
blocks.a:
• Turn the rule number into an 8-entry table: bit v of the rule is the output for neighbourhood v.
  • For every cell, encode its neighbourhood as one number: 4·left + 2·self + 1·right. np.correlate(row, [4, 2, 1], mode="same") does this for the whole row.
  • Look up all cells at once: new_row = table[codes].

blocks.q: What are Wolfram's four classes, and why is Class 4 the interesting one?
blocks.a:
• 1: dies to uniform; 2: simple stable/periodic patterns; 3: chaos (random-looking); 4: complex localised structures that move and interact.
  • Class 4 sits between order and chaos. Structures persist long enough to carry information and interact to process it, which is why Rule 110 can perform universal computation.

chapters.title: Game of Life
chapters.tagline: Two rules on a grid, gliders that walk, and a gun that broke a conjecture
goals: State Conway's rules and apply them to any cell by hand
Count all 8 neighbours of every cell at once with np.roll
Use the kernel-10 trick to turn "alive + neighbours" into one lookup
Explain what gliders, oscillators and the glider gun show about emergence

blocks.html:
Conway's Game of Life (1970) is a 2-D cellular automaton. Every cell is alive or dead and has 8 neighbours (including diagonals). Each step, all cells update at once:

  • Birth: a dead cell with exactly 3 live neighbours comes alive.
  • Survival: a live cell with 2 or 3 live neighbours stays alive.
  • Everyone else dies or stays dead (from loneliness or overcrowding).

That's all. From these two rules come still lifes, blinking oscillators, spaceships that glide across the grid, and machines that build other machines.
From the 3D world: in Life you predicted births and deaths, built a glider by hand, and fired the glider gun. Now you'll write the engine that runs it. Open Life

blocks.q: A live cell has 4 live neighbours. A dead cell has 2. What happens to each?

opts.t: The live cell dies (overcrowding); the dead cell stays dead
The live cell survives; the dead cell comes alive

blocks.why: Survival needs 2 or 3 neighbours, so 4 is too many. Birth needs exactly 3, so 2 is not enough.

blocks.html: We count neighbours with scipy.signal.correlate2d and a 3×3 kernel whose centre is 10 instead of 0. Then every cell gets one number: c = 10 × (alive?) + neighbours.     return ((c == 3) | (c == 12) | (c == 13)).astype(np.uint8)

sections.title: Real-world project: a pattern library that names what it sees

blocks.html: Life fans have catalogued hundreds of thousands of patterns, and nobody sorts them by hand: a program runs each one and classifies it. Is it a still life (never changes), an oscillator (comes back after k steps), a spaceship (comes back moved), or does it die? Writing that classifier is a lesson in a very common engineering problem: deciding when two states are "the same", even if one has moved.

blocks.title: Pattern detector for a Game of Life library
blocks.client: An online Life pattern wiki that wants to auto-tag uploads
blocks.brief: When someone uploads a pattern, the wiki should tag it automatically. Run it forward step by step and compare each state with the start. To spot a spaceship you need to compare shapes, not positions, so first write crop, which cuts a board down to the smallest box holding every live cell. Then classify returns ("dies", t), ("still life", 1), ("oscillator", period), ("spaceship", period) or ("unknown", 0).
blocks.why: Comparing states "up to a shift" is how image search finds a logo anywhere in a picture, how version-control tools spot moved code, and how simulators detect that a system has entered a cycle (a key trick in debugging and in model checkers that verify software). The real Life community runs exactly this kind of tool (apgsearch) over billions of random starts.

blocks.html:
Life also makes a philosophical point. Gliders "exist" at a higher level of description than cells. Are they real things, or just a convenient way to talk about cell patterns?

  • Realism: higher-level entities like gliders (or species, or economies) are real and the theories about them are true or false.
  • Instrumentalism: they're useful models; a theory is judged by how well it predicts, not whether it's "true".

Life also shows that simple rules can be universal: you can build logic gates from gliders, and Life is Turing complete.

blocks.q: Someone says: "Gliders aren't real. There are only cells turning on and off." Which point answers that?

opts.t: They're right; higher-level descriptions are errors
"Glider" is a valid, useful higher-level description, and the debate over whether it's "real" is the realism vs instrumentalism question
Gliders are real because they're in the source code
The rules of Life explicitly define gliders

blocks.why: Nothing in the two rules mentions gliders, yet "a glider moves one cell diagonally every 4 steps" predicts the system perfectly. Whether such emergent objects are "real" is exactly what realists and instrumentalists disagree about.

blocks.q: Explain the kernel-10 trick: why is "alive next step" the same as "c is 3, 12 or 13"?
blocks.a:
• The kernel adds up the 8 neighbours with weight 1 and the cell itself with weight 10, so c = 10·self + neighbours.
  • Dead cells have c = 0…8; live cells have c = 10…18. The two ranges can't overlap.
  • Birth (dead, 3 neighbours) → 3. Survival (alive, 2 or 3) → 12 or 13. Any other value means dead next step.

blocks.q: What did the glider gun prove, and why does it matter for complexity science?
blocks.a:
• Conway conjectured that every finite starting pattern eventually stops growing. The gun is a finite pattern whose population grows forever (one glider every 30 steps), so the conjecture is false.
  • It shows you often can't predict what simple rules will do by reasoning about them: you have to run them. And guns are a building block for computation in Life (glider streams as signals).

blocks.html:
Ink in water spreads because molecules jiggle randomly. On a grid, that becomes a simple rule: each step, every cell moves a little toward the average of its neighbours. The amount a cell differs from its neighbours is the Laplacian:

Δa = (up + down + left + right) − 4·a

and the update is a ← a + r·Δa for a small rate r. High spots fall, low spots rise, and everything smooths out.
From the 3D world: in Rock & ink you drilled through rock and grew Turing spots. The spots are the reaction–diffusion model here; the drilling is percolation. Open Rock & ink

blocks.html:
In 1952 Alan Turing proposed that two chemicals that react and diffuse at different speeds can form stable patterns: spots and stripes, like a leopard's coat. We use the Gray–Scott model with chemicals A and B:

  • A is fed in at rate f; B is removed at rate k;
  • the reaction A + 2B → 3B turns A into B where B already is;
  • A diffuses faster than B.

blocks.code:
def gray_scott(f, k, n=100, steps=5000):
    A = np.ones((n, n))
    B = np.zeros((n, n))
    A[40:60, 40:60] = 0.5           # a square seed in the middle
    B[40:60, 40:60] = 0.25

blocks.q: Describe the percolation model and what "critical porosity" means.
blocks.a:
• An n×n grid; each cell porous with probability q. Water starts in the top row and repeatedly spreads to porous neighbours.
  • The rock percolates if water reaches the bottom row.
  • Below about q = 0.593 large grids almost never percolate; above it they almost always do. That threshold is the critical value of a phase transition, and the transition gets sharper as n grows.

chapters.title: Self-organized criticality
chapters.tagline: Drop grains of sand one at a time and watch the pile tune itself to the edge
goals: Implement the Bak–Tang–Wiesenfeld sand pile's toppling rule with numpy
Relax a pile to stability and measure an avalanche's size and duration
Show that avalanche sizes follow a heavy-tailed distribution
Explain what "self-organized" criticality adds to the critical points of chapters 2 and 7
chapters.prelude:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def topple_step(a, K=3):
    """One round of toppling: every cell above K sends 1 grain to each of 4 neighbours.
    Grains pushed past the edge fall off the table."""
    toppling = a > K
    n = toppling.sum()
    t = toppling.astype(a.dtype)
    a -= 4 * t
    a[1:, :] += t[:-1, :]
    a[:-1, :] += t[1:, :]
    a[:, 1:] += t[:, :-1]
    a[:, :-1] += t[:, 1:]
    return n

blocks.html:
In chapters 2 and 7 you found critical points: a value of p or q where the system flips from one behaviour to another, with heavy tails and fractals right at the threshold. But someone had to set q to exactly 0.593. In nature, who does that?

In 1987 Bak, Tang and Wiesenfeld proposed an answer: some systems drive themselves to the critical point. Their model was a pile of sand. Keep dropping grains; the pile grows steeper until avalanches start; avalanches flatten it; it grows again. It ends up hovering at the edge, where the next grain might cause nothing, or might cause an avalanche of any size. That's self-organized criticality (SOC).
From the 3D world: in Sand you triggered avalanches by hand, collected 3,000 of them, and saw the pile settle near an average height of about 2.1 by itself. Open Sand

Each cell holds a number of grains. Any cell with more than K = 3 grains topples: it loses 4 and each of its 4 neighbours gains 1. Grains that would land off the edge are lost. Toppling can push neighbours over 3, so one topple can set off more: an avalanche.

def relax(a, K=3):
    duration = size = 0
    while (n := topple_step(a, K)):
        duration += 1
        size += n
    return duration, size

def drop(a, rng):
    i, j = rng.integers(a.shape[0]), rng.integers(a.shape[1])
    a[i, j] += 1
    return relax(a)

blocks.html:
SOC also says something about how we explain things. A reductionist explanation of an avalanche traces it to the grain that set it off and the cells it touched. But that misses the point: the same grain on the same cell might do nothing tomorrow. The holistic explanation is that the pile as a whole sits in a critical state, where small causes can have effects of any size.

SOC may explain heavy tails in earthquakes, forest fires, extinctions and even stock market crashes, with a warning that a heavy-tailed distribution alone doesn't prove SOC.

blocks.q: After a huge avalanche, someone asks "which grain caused it?" What does the SOC view say?

opts.t: The grain was only the trigger; the real cause is the pile's critical state, which made a large avalanche possible

blocks.why: In a critical system the size of the response is set by the state of the whole pile, not by the trigger. Asking which grain caused it is like asking which match caused a forest fire after decades of dry undergrowth.

blocks.html: Think of each cell as a substation and each grain as load. When a substation is pushed past its limit it trips, and its load is pushed onto its four neighbours, which may trip too. That is how real blackouts spread: in 2003 one overloaded line in Ohio cascaded into an outage for 50 million people. A grid run close to its limits behaves like your sand pile: most days nothing happens, and rarely, something enormous does.

blocks.solution:
def topple_step(a, K=3):
    toppling = a > K
    n = toppling.sum()
    t = toppling.astype(a.dtype)
    a -= 4 * t
    a[1:, :] += t[:-1, :]
    a[:-1, :] += t[1:, :]
    a[:, 1:] += t[:, :-1]
    a[:, :-1] += t[:, 1:]
    return n

blocks.q: What makes the sand pile "self-organized" critical, compared with percolation at q = 0.593?
blocks.a:
• In percolation, the critical point is a parameter value someone has to choose.
  • The sand pile reaches its critical state by itself: slow driving (one grain at a time) plus fast relaxation (avalanches) pushes it to the state where avalanches of all sizes occur.
  • Evidence: the average height settles near 2.1 whatever the start, and avalanche sizes and durations follow heavy-tailed distributions.

blocks.q: Describe the drop-and-relax experiment and what you measure.
blocks.a:
• Start with a tall pile and relax it to stability.
  • Repeatedly add one grain at a random cell and relax, counting the steps (duration) and total topples (size) of each avalanche.
  • Plot the distributions of size and duration on log-log axes (PMF or CCDF). A roughly straight line across a wide range is the heavy tail.

chapters.title: Agent-based models
chapters.tagline: Schelling's city in 2-D, then Sugarscape, where inequality grows out of simple foraging
goals: Name what makes a model "agent-based" and why heterogeneity matters

blocks.html:
Four features set agent-based models (ABMs) apart from the cellular automata of earlier chapters:

  • Agents that model people or organisms, each with its own state and simple behaviour.
  • Heterogeneity: agents differ from each other (here: how far they see, how fast they burn sugar).
  • An environment they live in and change.
  • Local interactions: agents only see and affect what's near them.

The interesting results are again emergent: segregation nobody asked for, and inequality nobody designed.
From the 3D world: in Sugar you survived as one agent, watched inequality emerge, tried a tax, and saw migration waves move diagonally. This chapter builds that world. Open Sugar

The classic version: an n×n grid; each cell is empty (0), red (1) or blue (2). An agent is unhappy if fewer than a fraction p of its 8 neighbours are the same colour as itself. Each step, every unhappy agent moves to a random empty cell.

blocks.code:
def frac_same(a):
    same, occ = np.zeros(a.shape), np.zeros(a.shape)
    for di in (-1, 0, 1):
        for dj in (-1, 0, 1):
            if (di, dj) != (0, 0):
                nb = np.roll(np.roll(a, di, 0), dj, 1)
                occ += nb != 0
                same += (nb == a) & (a != 0)
    with np.errstate(invalid="ignore", divide="ignore"):
        return np.where(occ > 0, same / occ, 1.0)

def step(a, p, rng):
    unhappy = (a != 0) & (frac_same(a) < p)
    movers = locs_where(unhappy)
    empties = locs_where(a == 0)
    rng.shuffle(movers)
    for src in movers:
        k = rng.integers(len(empties))
        dest = empties[k]
        a[dest], a[src] = a[src], 0
        empties[k] = src            # the old home is now empty
    return len(movers)

blocks.code:
def make_capacity(n=50):
    rows, cols = np.indices((n, n))
    dist = np.minimum(np.hypot(rows - 15, cols - 15), np.hypot(rows - 35, cols - 35))
    return np.digitize(dist, [21, 16, 11, 6]).astype(float)

def best_cell(sugar, loc, vision, occupied):
    n, m = sugar.shape
    r, c = loc
    cands = [(0, loc)]
    for dr, dc in [(-1, 0), (1, 0), (0, -1), (0, 1)]:
        for d in range(1, vision + 1):
            cell = ((r + dr * d) % n, (c + dc * d) % m)
            if cell not in occupied:
                cands.append((d, cell))
    return max(cands, key=lambda x: (sugar[x[1]], -x[0]))[1]

blocks.html:
The Gini coefficient is 0 when everyone has the same and approaches 1 when one agent has everything. One formula: sort the wealth values x₁ ≤ … ≤ xₙ, then

G = (2 Σᵢ i·xᵢ) / (n Σᵢ xᵢ) − (n + 1)/n, with i running from 1 to n.

def gini(wealth):
    x = np.sort(np.asarray(wealth, dtype=float))
    n = len(x)
    i = np.arange(1, n + 1)
    return 2 * np.sum(i * x) / (n * np.sum(x)) - (n + 1) / n

sections.title: Real-world project: a housing-policy what-if tool

blocks.html: Agent-based models are used for real policy work: transport planners, housing agencies and central banks run them to ask "what happens if we change this rule?" before trying it on real people. Here you'll turn Schelling's city into a small what-if tool and test one policy idea: anchored homes, like long-term social-housing tenancies, whose residents stay put whatever their neighbours look like.

blocks.why: This is how agent-based models earn their keep in practice: the UK's Bank of England uses them for the housing market, transport agencies use MATSim to test road pricing, and epidemiologists used them during COVID to compare lockdown rules. The software pattern is always the same: a model with knobs, a fixed seed so results can be reproduced and checked, and a sweep that turns runs into a chart someone can make a decision from.

sections.title: Boids: three rules make a flock

blocks.html:
Craig Reynolds (1987) animated flocks with agents he called boids. Each boid looks only at nearby boids and follows three rules:

  • Cohesion: steer toward the centre of your neighbours.
  • Separation: steer away from neighbours that are too close.
  • Alignment: steer toward your neighbours' average heading.

No boid knows the shape of the flock, and there is no leader. The flock emerges.

blocks.code:
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
n = 60
pos = rng.random((n, 2)) * 10
vel = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 2))

def neighbors(i, radius):
    d = np.linalg.norm(pos - pos[i], axis=1)
    return (d < radius) & (np.arange(n) != i)

def flock_step(dt=0.1):
    global pos, vel
    new = vel.copy()
    for i in range(n):
        near = neighbors(i, 2.0)
        if near.any():
            new[i] += 0.03 * (pos[near].mean(0) - pos[i])          # cohesion
            new[i] += 0.10 * (vel[near].mean(0) - vel[i])          # alignment
        close = neighbors(i, 0.5)
        if close.any():
            new[i] -= 0.20 * (pos[close].mean(0) - pos[i])         # separation
    speed = np.linalg.norm(new, axis=1, keepdims=True)
    vel = new / np.maximum(speed, 1e-9) * 2.0                      # constant speed
    pos = (pos + vel * dt) % 10

def order():
    """1 when everyone flies the same way, near 0 when headings are random."""
    return np.linalg.norm(vel.mean(0)) / 2.0

print("alignment at start:", round(order(), 2))
for _ in range(200):
    flock_step()
print("alignment after 200 steps:", round(order(), 2))

sections.title: Real-world project: how many cars should a ring road carry?

blocks.html: Traffic engineers have a chart called the fundamental diagram: put more cars on a road and the flow (cars passing a point per minute) first rises, then falls, because jams appear. The peak tells them the road's real capacity, which is where ramp-metering lights (the traffic lights on motorway on-ramps) try to hold the road. Your highway model can draw that chart.

blocks.title: Capacity study for a ring road
blocks.client: A city transport department deciding when to switch on ramp-metering lights
blocks.brief:
For each number of cars on the ring, run the model, throw away the warm-up, and measure the flow: density (cars per unit of road) times average speed. Then find the number of cars that gives the most flow. That number is the trigger for the ramp lights: above it, letting more cars on makes everyone slower and moves fewer people.

One change from the chapter's model: real cars take up road, so here each car is 5 units long and never drives closer than that to the car ahead. Without a length, a ring of 1,000 units could hold a million cars and never jam.
blocks.why: Ramp metering, congestion pricing and the variable speed limits on smart motorways are all designed around the fundamental diagram. The same "throughput rises then collapses" curve shows up in software: a web server or database handles more requests per second as load rises, until contention makes throughput fall, which is why load balancers and rate limiters cap concurrency at the peak.

blocks.setup:
def gaps(locs, L, car_length=5):
    return (np.roll(locs, -1) - locs) % L - car_length  # free road ahead, minus the car itself

def step(locs, speeds, L, rng, eps=0.0, max_acc=1, speed_limit=40):
    gap = gaps(locs, L)
    speeds = np.clip(speeds + max_acc, 0, speed_limit)
    slow = rng.random(len(speeds)) < eps
    speeds = np.where(slow, np.maximum(speeds - rng.uniform(0, 8, len(speeds)), 0), speeds)
    speeds = np.clip(np.minimum(speeds, gap), 0, None)  # never drive into the car in front
    return (locs + speeds) % L, speeds

def flow(n_cars, L=1000, steps=200, eps=0.02, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    locs = np.linspace(0, L, n_cars, endpoint=False)
    speeds = np.zeros(n_cars)
    ms = []
    for _ in range(steps):

        ms.append(speeds.mean())
    return (n_cars / L) * np.mean(ms[steps // 2:])

blocks.q: Explain why one driver briefly braking can create a jam that lasts and moves backward.
blocks.a:
• The car behind sees a smaller gap and must slow down too, slightly later; then the car behind it, and so on. The slowdown propagates upstream.
  • Each car takes time to accelerate back up, so cars leave the front of the slow region more slowly than new cars arrive at its back when traffic is dense.
  • The slow region (the jam) is a pattern that moves backward, even though every car moves forward.

chapters.tagline: Replicators, variation and selection on a fitness landscape, one ingredient at a time
goals: Name the three ingredients evolution needs, and show what breaks without each one

chapters.prelude:
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

blocks.html:
Take a minimal view. Evolution happens whenever you have:

  1. Replicators: things that make copies of themselves.
  2. Variation: copies aren't all identical (mutation).
  3. Differential survival or reproduction: some variants do better than others.

Nothing about DNA or living things is required. That's why we can study evolution with a simulation of bit strings, and switch each ingredient off to see what it does.
From the 3D world: in Evolution you turned the ingredients on and off, changed the environment, and watched a new species form. Here is the code underneath. Open Evolution

blocks.q: A population copies itself perfectly (no mutation) and some genotypes reproduce faster than others. What happens over a long time?

opts.t: The best genotype already present takes over, then nothing changes

blocks.why: Selection only chooses among existing variants. Without new variation the fittest starting genotype eventually dominates and evolution stops. You'll see this in the simulation.

blocks.html:
A genome is a string of N bits (with N = 8 there are 2⁸ = 256 possible genotypes; the simulation below uses N = 16, so 65,536). Each position contributes to fitness, and the contribution depends on whether that bit is 0 or 1. We draw two random numbers per position, zero_values[i] and one_values[i], and fitness is the average contribution:

fitness(loc) = mean over i of (one_values[i] if loc[i] == 1 else zero_values[i])

blocks.code:
class FitnessLandscape:
    def __init__(self, N, rng):
        self.N = N
        self.one_values = rng.random(N)
        self.zero_values = rng.random(N)
    def fitness(self, loc):
        return np.mean(np.where(loc, self.one_values, self.zero_values))

def run(landscape, rng, n=100, gens=400, selection=True, p_mutate=0.2, start="worst", strength=8):
    N = landscape.N
    worst = (landscape.one_values < landscape.zero_values).astype(int)
    pop = [worst.copy() if start == "worst" else rng.integers(0, 2, N) for _ in range(n)]
    mean_fit = []
    for g in range(gens):
        fits = np.array([landscape.fitness(x) for x in pop])
        mean_fit.append(fits.mean())
        dead = np.flatnonzero(rng.random(n) < 0.2)
        weights = fits ** strength                  # exaggerate fitness differences
        p = weights / weights.sum() if selection else None
        parents = rng.choice(n, size=len(dead), p=p)
        for d, par in zip(dead, parents):
            child = pop[par].copy()
            if rng.random() < p_mutate:
                i = rng.integers(N); child[i] = 1 - child[i]
            pop[d] = child
    return mean_fit

best = np.mean(np.maximum(landscape.one_values, landscape.zero_values))
runs = [("selection + mutation", {}),
        ("no mutation, random start", {"p_mutate": 0, "start": "random"}),
        ("no mutation, identical start", {"p_mutate": 0}),
        ("no selection", {"selection": False})]
for label, kw in runs:

    plt.plot(curve, label=label)

blocks.q: "No mutation, random start" rises quickly and then goes flat below the best possible fitness, while "no mutation, identical start" never moves at all. Why?

opts.t: Selection used up the variation that was there at the start; with no new variants it can't climb higher
Mutation is required for any change at all

blocks.why: With a random start there's plenty of variation, so selection improves fitness at first. Once the population converges on the best of what existed, there's nothing new to select. With an identical start there's no variation at all, so selection has nothing to act on. Mutation supplies the novelty that keeps the climb going.

blocks.q: "No selection" drifts up from the worst genome to about the middle (roughly 0.5) and then wanders, far below the peak. Which ingredient is missing?

opts.t: Replication; the population can't copy itself
Differential reproduction; without it, mutation just causes random drift, not adaptation
Nothing is missing; this is normal evolution

blocks.why: Copies and mutations still happen, so the population changes, but nothing favours fitter variants. It drifts toward a typical random genome (average fitness), not toward the peak. Adaptation needs selection and variation together.

sections.title: Real-world project: evolve a delivery route

blocks.html: You've seen evolution climb a fitness landscape with nothing but copying, variation and selection. Engineers borrow that recipe as a genetic algorithm when a problem has far too many options to try them all. A van that visits 12 shops has about 20 million possible round trips; 20 shops, over 10¹⁷. Instead of checking them all, breed good routes from good routes.

def evolve_route(pts, gens=200, n=60, seed=0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    pop = [rng.permutation(len(pts)) for _ in range(n)]
    best = min(pop, key=lambda o: route_length(o, pts))
    for g in range(gens):
        lengths = np.array([route_length(o, pts) for o in pop])
        fits = (1 / lengths) ** 8
        dead = np.flatnonzero(rng.random(n) < 0.2)
        parents = rng.choice(n, size=len(dead), p=fits / fits.sum())
        for d, par in zip(dead, parents):
            pop[d] = reverse_segment(pop[par], rng)
        cand = min(pop, key=lambda o: route_length(o, pts))
        if route_length(cand, pts) < route_length(best, pts):
            best = cand.copy()
    return best

blocks.q: What are the three ingredients of evolution in the minimal view, and what happens when you remove variation or selection?
blocks.a:
• Replicators, variation, differential survival or reproduction.
  • No variation (no mutation): selection quickly picks the best existing genotype, then fitness stops rising.
  • No selection: mutation causes random drift; fitness wanders but doesn't climb.
  • Only with all three does the population keep adapting toward a peak.

blocks.q: Why choose replacements with probability proportional to fitness instead of always copying the single best agent?
blocks.a:
• It models differential reproduction realistically: fitter agents tend to have more offspring, but luck still matters.
  • It keeps variation in the population longer, so evolution can explore instead of collapsing onto one genotype immediately.

import numpy as np

blocks.html:
Two suspects are questioned separately. Each can cooperate (stay silent) or defect (betray the other). In points:

other cooperatesother defects
you cooperate3 (reward)0 (sucker)
you defect5 (temptation)1 (punishment)

Whatever the other player does, you score more by defecting. So both defect and get 1 each, when they could have had 3 each. Rational individuals produce a bad collective outcome. Then how does cooperation, which is everywhere in nature and society, ever evolve?

""first round: nothing seen yet

"CC", "CD", "DC", "DD"later rounds: the opponent's last two moves

So a genome is a list of 7 moves, e.g. tit for tat: cooperate first, then copy the opponent's last move: ["C", "C", "D", "C", "D", "C", "D"].

blocks.q: Tit for tat never scores more than its opponent in a single match (it lost 5–10 to all-D). Yet in Axelrod's 1980 tournaments it had the highest total score. How?

opts.t: It does well against cooperators (18 each) and loses only a little to defectors, so its average across all opponents is high
It beats every strategy head to head

blocks.why: Head-to-head wins don't matter; total points across all games do. All-D beats everyone it meets, but scores poorly overall because nobody cooperates with it. Tit for tat earns full cooperation from nice strategies and limits its losses against nasty ones.

blocks.html:
Now the experiment. Start with 100 agents that always defect. Each generation:

  1. every agent plays iterated games against 2 others,
  2. its fitness is its average score,
  3. 10% die at random and are replaced by copies of agents chosen in proportion to fitness,
  4. each copy mutates one random gene with probability 0.05.

We track niceness: the fraction of all genes in the population that are "C".

blocks.code:
def respond(genome, opp_history):
    return genome[KEYS.index("".join(opp_history[-2:]))]

def play(g1, g2, rounds=6):
    h1, h2, s1, s2 = [], [], 0, 0
    for _ in range(rounds):
        m1, m2 = respond(g1, h2), respond(g2, h1)
        a, b = PAYOFF[(m1, m2)]
        s1, s2 = s1 + a, s2 + b
        h1.append(m1); h2.append(m2)
    return s1, s2

def evolve(gens=800, n=100, p_mutate=0.05, seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    pop = [["D"] * 7 for _ in range(n)]
    niceness, mean_score = [], []
    for g in range(gens):
        total, games = np.zeros(n), np.zeros(n)
        order = rng.permutation(n)
        for k in range(n):
            for off in (1, 2):                      # play 2 neighbours on a shuffled ring
                i, j = order[k], order[(k + off) % n]
                a, b = play(pop[i], pop[j])
                total[i] += a; total[j] += b; games[i] += 1; games[j] += 1
        fit = total / games
        mean_score.append(fit.mean())
        niceness.append(np.mean([x.count("C") / 7 for x in pop]))
        dead = np.flatnonzero(rng.random(n) < 0.1)
        parents = rng.choice(n, size=len(dead), p=fit / fit.sum())
        for d, par in zip(dead, parents):
            child = list(pop[par])
            if rng.random() < p_mutate:
                i = rng.integers(7)
                child[i] = "C" if child[i] == "D" else "D"
            pop[d] = child
    return niceness, mean_score, pop

blocks.html:
Axelrod's analysis of his tournaments found the successful strategies shared a few traits:

  • Nice: never the first to defect.
  • Retaliating: punish defection, so you can't be exploited forever.
  • Forgiving: return to cooperation when the other does.
  • Clear: easy for others to recognise and adapt to.

None of this needs altruism. In the repeated game, cooperating with reciprocators simply pays. Once a few reciprocators exist, they score well with each other, and selection does the rest.

blocks.q: Why can a mutant cooperator in an all-defector population not take off alone, while a small cluster of reciprocators can?

opts.t: A lone cooperator only meets defectors and gets exploited; reciprocators that meet each other earn 18 instead of 6 and outscore defectors
Defectors refuse to play with cooperators

blocks.why: Cooperation pays only when cooperators meet each other. That's why it often appears in waves: a few reciprocators drift in, find each other, out-earn defectors, and spread.

sections.title: Real-world project: a tournament for negotiation bots

blocks.html: Axelrod ran his famous tournaments by inviting people to send in strategies and playing them all against each other. You can run the same thing. Think of each genome as a negotiation bot: cooperate means "make a fair offer", defect means "grab more". The twist that real negotiators know: messages get misread. A fair offer sometimes looks like a grab. That noise changes which bots win.

blocks.title: Round-robin tournament for negotiation bots
blocks.client: A course on negotiation that wants students to submit bots and see them compete
blocks.brief: Build the tournament engine. round_robin(bots) plays every pair of bots once and returns each bot's total score. play_noisy is play with a twist: each move is flipped with probability noise before the other player sees it. Then compare the leaderboard with and without noise: does tit for tat still win when messages get garbled?
blocks.why: Tournaments like this are how AI researchers compare game-playing agents (from Axelrod's 1980 contest to poker bots and multi-agent benchmarks), and the noisy version is why real protocols include forgiveness: TCP backs off and retries instead of giving up on a dropped packet, and diplomats use hotlines to explain a misread signal before it escalates. Round-robin scheduling itself is everywhere, from sports fixtures to load testing every pair of services.
milestones: Write round_robin(bots, rounds): every pair plays once, totals go into a dict
Print a leaderboard sorted by score
Write play_noisy: flip each move with probability noise
Show that tit for tat against itself breaks into long feuds when there is noise
Add a forgiving bot that only punishes two defections in a row, and see if it beats tit for tat under noise
stretch: Let students submit bots as Python functions instead of 7-gene lists
Run an evolutionary tournament: after each round, bots reproduce in proportion to their score
Report, for each pair, who won the head-to-head and by how much

blocks.title: round_robin
blocks.prompt: Write round_robin(bots, rounds=6). bots is a dict mapping a name to a genome. Play every pair of different bots once with play(g1, g2, rounds) (no bot plays itself), add each player's score to its total, and return a dict of totals. play is defined.

bots = {"always C": ["C"] * 7, "always D": ["D"] * 7, "tit for tat": ["C", "C", "D", "C", "D", "C", "D"]}

The flipped move is what gets scored and what goes into the history (it's what the other side saw). blocks.solution:
def play(g1, g2, rounds=6):
    h1, h2 = [], []
    s1 = s2 = 0
    for _ in range(rounds):
        m1 = g1[KEYS.index("".join(h2[-2:]))]
        m2 = g2[KEYS.index("".join(h1[-2:]))]
        a, b = PAYOFF[(m1, m2)]
        s1 += a
        s2 += b
        h1.append(m1)
        h2.append(m2)
    return s1, s2

blocks.q: Explain how cooperation can evolve in a population that starts out all defectors, using the iterated prisoner's dilemma.
blocks.a:
• In a single game defection dominates, but in repeated games strategies can condition on history.
  • Mutation occasionally produces reciprocating strategies (nice but retaliating, like tit for tat).
  • When reciprocators meet each other they cooperate and earn far more than defectors earn against each other (18 vs 6 over 6 rounds), while losing little against defectors.
  • Fitness-proportional reproduction spreads them, so niceness and average score rise, often in waves, without anyone being altruistic.

blocks.q: List Axelrod's traits of successful strategies.
blocks.a: • Nice (never defect first), retaliating (punish defection), forgiving (return to cooperation), and clear (easy for others to read).
